::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Proof with exponent](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4854151/proof-with-exponent), asked by [Maya](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1242454/maya) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2024-01-31; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> How do I prove that
>
> $$1+be^b \leq e^b$$
>
> If I know that $b\geq0$.
>
> My idea:
>
> I thought writing it as $f(x) = 1+be^b - e^b$. Derivative of this function is $f'(x) = be^b$. We have minima at $b=0$.
:::

Consider the function $f(x) = e^x$ on the interval $[0,b]$. By the mean value theorem there exists $c$ such that $0 < c < b$ and $$\frac{f(b)-f(0)}{b-0} = f'(c)$$

The left-hand side is $\frac{e^b-1}{b}$ and the right-hand side is $e^c$, which is $\leq e^b$. Therefore,
$$\frac{e^b-1}{b} \leq e^b \implies e^b - 1 \leq be^b \implies e^b \leq 1 + be^b$$
